meta.description: The subtlest layer. Human writing carries traces of cognitive processes that AI cannot replicate: cognitive load fluctuations, self-monitoring artifacts, and lexical retrieval signatures. These are not things to 'add' mechanically but patterns to allow through rather than polish away.
meta.usage: Sixth and final layer pass (after content_profile adjustments). Call humanizer_get_psycholinguistic_texture. Apply this layer LAST. Its concrete-action rewriting_guidance is in tension with most prior layers' polish; the AI tendency to over-polish is what this layer fights. The right LLM behavior here is restraint, which means keeping what the source has and adding nothing it lacks. In particular, do not flatten the source's self-corrections, do not balance every clause, and do not normalize its lexical retrieval near-misses if they preserve meaning. See caveats.uniform_application_paradox.
meta.research_basis: Opara (2025) mapped 31 stylometric features to four psycholinguistic theories: Cognitive Load Theory, Metacognition and Self-Monitoring, Lexical Access and Retrieval, and Discourse Planning and Cohesion. This framework explains why specific stylometric features serve as effective discriminators.

cognitive_load_artifacts.theory: Human working memory has limited capacity. When writing tasks overwhelm this capacity, performance changes and error likelihood increases. This strain manifests in natural markers (simplification, omission, and stylistic fluctuation). AI does not experience cognitive load; its output is uniformly polished.
human_markers: Sentence simplification after complex passages: a long, dense sentence followed by a noticeably simpler one
Shorter words in high-information-density passages; humans conserve cognitive resources
Occasional repetition of a word used in the previous sentence when the writer's focus is on the argument, not the prose
rewriting_guidance: Do not raise every paragraph to the same density. When a dense passage is followed by a plainer one, leave the plainer one plain.
Don't develop every point to the same depth. A secondary point can be stated once and left, as long as every claim the source makes is still there.

Inside dense technical passages, prefer the shorter, plainer word. 'The algorithm works by checking each node' reads more human than 'The algorithm functions by evaluating each node' when the surrounding context is already complex.

self_monitoring_traces.theory: Human writers engage in metacognitive monitoring; they evaluate their own text as they write, adjusting tone, correcting course, and responding to their own arguments. This self-monitoring produces visible artifacts: abrupt stylistic changes, mid-course corrections, and context-sensitive modifications. AI lacks this metacognitive capability.
human_markers: Mid-paragraph tone shifts where the writer catches themselves being too formal or too casual
Self-corrections ('or rather', 'to be more precise') where the writer changed course mid-thought. They belong to the source; a staged one reads as performance.
Parenthetical qualifications that interrupt the main argument to add nuance
Inconsistent punctuation use that drifts over the course of a document (selective Oxford commas, parentheses used in some sections and not others)
Questions the writer asks of their own argument, where the source reasons aloud. A one-line question added for effect reads as a model's tic.
Contractions used in some sentences but not others, reflecting natural register drift
rewriting_guidance: Allow the CHOICE of punctuation to drift among valid options. If the first half uses Oxford commas and the second half sometimes drops them, leave it. Drift never means omitting required punctuation, dropping terminal marks, or using marks incorrectly (see absolute_rules AR-003).
Keep the source's contractions where they are. Uneven use is normal in human writing, so do not even it out or manufacture it.

lexical_retrieval_signatures.theory: Word selection in human writing involves a complex interplay between semantics, grammar, memory, and personal experience. This cognitive process can result in occasional retrieval quirks: near-misses, contextually unusual but defensible choices, and vocabulary that reflects the writer's specific background rather than a generic register.
human_markers: Domain-specific vocabulary that reflects the writer's actual expertise, not generic formal words
Occasional informal or colloquial words mixed into formal prose when the writer's natural voice breaks through
Idioms that come from the writer's own speech rather than a stock list
Words chosen for their exact meaning, which are often not the most probable next token
Proper nouns and specific references drawn from the writer's knowledge rather than generic categories
rewriting_guidance: Replace generic formal words with vocabulary that reflects the author's actual domain. A software engineer writes 'race condition' not 'concurrent access issue.'
Keep an idiom the source already uses; don't add one to sound human.
Let the occasional informal word survive in formal prose. A 'clunky interface' in a technical report signals a human judgment that 'an interface with suboptimal usability' does not.
Keep the specific names, places and references the source gives. Do not generalize 'the 737 MAX groundings' into 'a recent aviation incident.'

discourse_planning_traces.theory: Effective writing requires logical progression of ideas. Human writers build narratives hierarchically, from broad ideas to fine-grained detail. But under cognitive load, this planning may falter, leading to abrupt topic changes, uneven development, or weak transitions that the writer didn't go back to fix.
human_markers: Occasional topic shifts that feel slightly abrupt; the writer moved on before fully closing the previous point
Uneven development: some ideas get three paragraphs, others get one sentence, reflecting the writer's sense of what matters
Implied transitions where the connection between ideas is clear but not explicitly stated
Occasional tangential observations that are relevant but break the strict logical flow
rewriting_guidance: Give more space to the ideas that matter most. A model gives every point equal airtime by default.
Keep asides the source has. Do not invent a tangent to make the text sound human.
Leave some transitions implicit. The reader can often follow the logic without a bridge sentence.
Vary the granularity of argument. Some points deserve detailed evidence. Others can be asserted and moved on from. AI tends to develop every point to the same depth.
